note.question: How can a seller run an efficient and approximately incentive-compatible auction when bids and payments lie on a fixed price grid and bidders' willingness to pay changes with wealth?
note.overview: This is a mechanism-design and market-design paper. Unit-demand agents with private classical utility functions participate in a multiobject auction; the paper defines a tight equilibrium, constructs a descending-price mechanism that implements it, and proves efficiency and approximate incentive compatibility.

components.label: Tight equilibrium implemented by a sequential descending-price auction
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Tight equilibrium implemented by a sequential descending-price auction. A tight equilibrium is a discrete equilibrium satisfying local connectedness and no improvement cycles. Theorem 1 implements one by the sequential descending auction, and Theorem 2 proves its allocation is efficient.

sources.quote: Each tight equilibrium is a locally optimal discrete equilibrium in which no local welfare improvement of either type is possible, as demonstrated above.14 These two conditions offer an intuitive way to move from a discrete equilibrium to a tight equilibrium: recursively reducing the price of a single object or eliminating an improvement cycle at the given price.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: The seller fixes a price increment epsilon and initializes high personalized prices. The sequential descending auction lowers prices along a monotone path; agents reveal only partial demand or strict-preference information, prices and tentative assignments are adjusted, and improvement cycles are executed until a tight equilibrium allocation and payment vector is reached. Discrete prices can destroy existence of a Walrasian equilibrium, so tight equilibrium permits one-increment demand tolerance while imposing local improvement structure. The descending path performs price discovery without requiring full preference reports.
